w: One hundred and twenty-seven miles of canal, ninety-one locks, and a climb clean over the Pennines -- built to haul goods between two rival northern cities before the railways made it obsolete. It still threads through Leeds today, and picked up a new link into the Liverpool docks this century.
s: 127 miles of canal, 91 locks, straight over the Pennines
_facts: 127-mile canal linking Leeds and Liverpool, crossing the Pennines
Has 91 locks on its main line
Gained a new link into the Liverpool docks system in the early 21st century

w: A Tudor-Jacobean house with grounds laid out by Capability Brown himself, tucked into the east side of Leeds where you'd least expect a stately home. It's Grade I listed and now runs as one of the city's museums -- a slice of aristocratic parkland the industrial heartland kept intact.
s: A Capability Brown estate hiding in industrial Leeds
_facts: Tudor-Jacobean house with grounds landscaped by Capability Brown
One of eight Leeds Museums and Galleries sites
Part of the Yorkshire Country House Partnership research group

w: The national collection of arms and armour used to live entirely in the Tower of London -- then in 1996 a chunk of it moved here, into a purpose-built £42.5 million museum on Leeds Dock. Suits of armour and centuries of edged steel, and it's still free to walk in.
s: The Tower of London's armour collection, moved to Leeds
_facts: Holds the National Collection of Arms and Armour
Part of the Royal Armouries family alongside the Tower of London and Fort Nelson
A £42.5 million purpose-built museum at Leeds Dock that opened in 1996
Entry is free, as at all UK National Museums

w: They called them Tom Puddings -- trains of compartment boats, first floated in the 1860s, that carried coal down this canalised river to be tipped straight into ships by giant hydraulic hoists. At its peak the system moved over 1.5 million tons of coal a year; it wasn't abandoned until 1986.
s: Tom Puddings: coal barges hoisted straight into ships
_facts: Canalised section of the Rivers Aire and Calder, improved from 1704
1860s 'Tom Pudding' compartment boats carried coal, unloaded into ships by hydraulic hoists
At its peak carried more than 1.5 million tons of coal a year
The coal-carrying system was not abandoned until 1986
